desc:
Given an integer array nums and a non-negative integer d, count the pairs of positions (i, j) with i < j whose values differ by at most d: |nums[i] - nums[j]| ≤ d.

Pairs at different positions are counted separately even when their values are equal.

nums = [1, 5, 3, 9, 4], d = 2
sorted: 1 3 4 5 9
pairs: (1,3) (3,4) (3,5) (4,5)
result = 4

nums = [7, 7, 7, 2], d = 0
result = 3
hints: Only the values matter, not the positions, so you can reorder the array. What does sorting give you?
In a sorted array, the partners of a[j] among earlier elements form a contiguous block ending at j - 1.
Keep a left pointer l. For each j move l forward while a[j] - a[l] > d; all indices l..j-1 are partners, so add j - l. The pointer never moves backwards, because a[j] only grows.
editorial: After sorting, a[j] - a[k] is non-increasing in k for a fixed j, so the earlier elements within distance d form a suffix of the prefix a[0..j-1], starting at the first index l with a[j] - a[l] ≤ d. Counting them is just j - l.

When j increases, a[j] does not decrease, so the first acceptable index l cannot move left. Two monotone pointers therefore cover the array in O(n) after the O(n log n) sort. The answer is at most n(n-1)/2, about 12.5 million, which fits in 32 bits.
